H1-P4.a: In the villages and families I've spent time around, land, childcare, housing, food, obligations, etc etc often go through the extended family and through local memory, along with the formal systems. Who needs a "Rebuilding Intergenerational Belonging" workshop when all it takes is some aunt giving three people a task?
H1-P4.c: In the villages and families I've spent time around, so much is taken care of by the extended family and the local memory, alongside the formal systems. Whether it's land, childcare, housing, food, obligations, etc, etc. Who needs a workshop called "Rebuilding Intergenerational Belonging" when some aunt has already given three people a task?

H3-P2.plain: But these days it can be soul destroying. People have a lot less of the communal life that held the obligation up, but they still carry it. So if one of them makes it into the cash economy, it's really hard to become independent or start a stable life, because they're expected to carry everybody. How can they get ahead, when all these people are dependent on them? And the relatives stay dependent too, since the payments don't give them a real alternative. It's the ancestral ethic playing out inside an individualistic cash economy. It can keep people alive, but it eats away at both sides too.
H3-P2.l: But these days it can be soul destroying. People have a lot less of the communal life that held the obligation up (the shared land, work, childcare, food and daily belonging), but they still carry it. So if one of them makes it into the cash economy, it's really hard to become independent or start a stable life, because they're expected to carry everybody. How can they get ahead, when all these people are dependent on them? And the relatives stay dependent too, since the payments don't give them a real alternative. It's the ancestral ethic playing out inside an individualistic cash economy. It can keep people alive, but it eats away at both sides too.
